1:
Every witness marks a turning point. Barnes says the chapter opens an important part of the history: until now the apostles had preached to Jews only, keeping their nation’s conviction that salvation was not offered beyond it, whereas the tendency of the Christian religion was to enlarge the mind. Henry calls the bringing in of the Gentiles so much a mystery to the apostles themselves that we must observe every circumstance of the work’s beginning. Calvin states the paradox: God advances a stranger, uncircumcised, to a singular honour above all the Jews, sending an angel to him and bringing Peter to Caesarea for his sake. Ellicott suggests Luke had the details from Philip the Evangelist at Caesarea, or from Cornelius himself, and observes that this admission became the ruling case on the question. Wesley draws a pattern: Caesarea was the seat of civil government as Jerusalem was of the ecclesiastical, the gospel making its way first through the metropolitan cities. Robertson notes the contrasts Furneaux draws between old Joppa and Herod’s Caesarea, and between the Galilean fisherman lodging with a tanner and the Roman officer in the seat of power.

What Cornelius was religiously is the first dispute. Barnes denies the terms make him a Jew or proselyte at all, holding there may have been a few Gentiles who feared God and maintained his worship by the light they had. Robertson takes the two phrases as Luke’s standing description of a God-fearing proselyte who had entered synagogue worship without circumcision. Ellicott agrees the word for devout marks the devotion of Gentile converts to Judaism; Gill says only that he had forsaken the Roman idolatry in which he was brought up. Clarke works from etymology, one who worships the true God and is no idolater, taking the fear of God as knowing him by his word and laws. Chrysostom presses that rank is not the reason for the pains taken over either man — this centurion or the eunuch at Gaza — but piety, scripture mentioning their stations to show how much greater piety is in such a station. Calvin sums the virtues as those in which the integrity of the godly consists, his life framed to the rule God prescribes; Ellicott finds significance in the centurion’s not being content with a higher truth for himself alone, Clarke that he established God’s worship in his house. Wesley notes the alms were given to the Jews, many of whom were then extremely poor.

On the vision the concern is to rule out illusion. Gill insists he was neither dreaming nor in a trance but awake in clear day; Wesley says the same, not in a trance like Peter but plainly, leaving no room to suspect imposition; Clarke calls the text as plain as can be that an angel appeared, at an hour precluding sleep. Calvin makes the timing the safeguard, since men are often deceived by juggling and Luke sets down the hour to avoid suspicion, so that this was fair daylight. Ellicott takes the adverb as distinguishing this from a dream like Joseph’s or a trance like Peter’s. Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott identify the hour as three in the afternoon and a stated time of prayer, Ellicott adding that Cornelius had so far accepted the Jewish rules of devotion, the Law being for him too a schoolmaster. Robertson notes the participle is ingressive, so he saw the angel come rather than coming.

Gill accounts for the fear by the brightness of the clothing and the majestic form, observing that such fear was usual with good men — the patriarchs and prophets, Zacharias, the Virgin Mary. Barnes argues the word rendered Lord should have been Sir, since nothing shows this an address to God or that Cornelius took the figure for the Lord; it is what a man would say when surprised by a strange form before him.
5:
Calvin notices what the angel does not do. God dealt favourably with Cornelius in not commanding him to travel but only to send, so that he stayed at home while Peter endured the journey for his sake; nor is such courtesy strange, since God daily thrusts the ministers of his word upon the unwilling and appears of his own accord to those who do not seek him. The harder question he raises himself: why did the angel not simply teach the man, instead of sending him for a fisherman? On the obedience that follows he makes the promptness the point — Cornelius made no tarriance but did with all diligence what he was commanded, and he was so forward because he believed the promise, as want of faith is the reason we are slow to follow God. Angels do not come flying from heaven to appoint us particular men, but the voice of Christ sounds in every ear: seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened. Gill reads the same readiness in the narrative: as soon as the angel withdrew Cornelius showed himself ready to obey, and he told the messengers the whole matter partly to send them the more cheerfully and partly so they could give Peter a distinct account.

The lodging draws practical comment. Barnes explains that tanneries are built on the margin of water to carry off the filth of dressing skins, Joppa being a seaport; Robertson adds that the house lay outside the walls for that trade, and that some tanneries stand by the shore at Jaffa still. Gill supposes Simon the tanner was very probably a good man and one who lodged strangers. Robertson glosses the verb for lodging from the word for a stranger received as a guest, and notes that the verb for fetching Peter is middle, of sending another on one’s own account, and occurs only in Acts.

Clarke reads the promise that Peter shall tell him what he ought to do as evidence about Cornelius’s state of mind: matters of great moment had occupied him, he was satisfied neither with the state of his own soul nor with the degree of religious knowledge he had, and he had set apart a particular time for extraordinary fasting and prayer that God might reveal more of his will — perhaps having heard of Jesus and been perplexed by the different opinions about him.

The messengers themselves are read as further evidence of the man. Barnes calls the soldier an instance of the effect of piety in a military officer, since few men have more influence, and it appears not only in the centurion’s family but in his attendant; such men are usually supposed far from religion, but this shows the labours of a camp are not necessarily hostile to it. Clarke makes the same inference about the regiment, and remarks that it was not then reckoned a disgrace even among the Romans for an officer to teach his men morality and piety toward God, whatever it may be in some Christian countries now. Wesley turns the phrase into a complaint about his own day: how many such attendants have our modern officers? A devout soldier, he says, would now be looked on as little better than a deserter from his colours. Ellicott holds the word describing the soldier implies he was, like his officer, a convert to the faith of Israel without being a full proselyte, and infers the same of the two servants, to whom their master told a vision that heathens would have found strange. Clarke closes with an observation Barnes repeats after him: that from Joppa Jonah was sent to preach to the Gentiles of Nineveh, and from the same place Peter was now sent to preach to the Gentiles at Caesarea.
9:
The journey is measured four ways: Gill thirty-six miles, checking Josephus, who gives a hundred and fifty furlongs to Antipatris and twenty-six miles thence; Ellicott about thirty Roman miles; Robertson twenty-eight; Clarke twelve or fifteen leagues. Clarke adds from Calmet that they must have travelled part of the night to arrive towards noon, and explains the party — two servants sent out of respect to Peter, the soldier probably for defence. Robertson lays out the four days.

On the hour and the place the agreement is close. Barnes says the roof or upper room was the usual place for prayer, and that though the Jews had two stated seasons the more pious added a third about noon, as David prayed evening, morning and at noon. Ellicott finds Peter again keeping the Jewish hours, and infers from the hunger that he had eaten nothing, making this probably one of the two weekly fast days. Calvin sets the two visions side by side and concludes the whole matter was governed by the wonderful counsel of God, who makes Cornelius apt to be taught while making Peter willing to teach. Henry names the obstacle the second vision removes: Cornelius has orders to send, but whether Peter will come is another question — not that he thought it beneath him, nor that he feared to preach to a man of that standing, but that it sticks at a point of conscience.

The hunger and the vision are connected by nearly everyone, and the connection is the most interesting thing in the passage. Wesley states it as a rule, that the symbols in visions and trances are generally suited to the state of the natural faculties. Ellicott says the vision’s form corresponded with the Apostle’s bodily condition, and allows the trance might in part follow from fasting, intense prayer and the noontide sun. Robertson notes Peter may even have smelt the dishes being made ready, and quotes the remark that the natural and the supernatural border closely on one another with no definable limits. Gill observes that those were reckoned most religious who ate nothing before the afternoon prayer; Clarke, that the ancients had no breakfast and only a slight dinner, supper being the principal meal; Barnes gives the two meals as about ten or eleven and six or seven. Robertson notes the word for hungry occurs nowhere else, and that the verb for desiring is imperfect, a longing to eat. Calvin puts the trance to another use: because our minds are set wholly on the earth, Peter’s had to be carried up, and so prepared to receive the oracle.

Two witnesses insist the language is figurative. Barnes derives the opening of heaven from a Hebrew way of speaking, as though the sky were a solid expanse that could be opened, and marks “as it had been” as important, since the writer does not say Peter literally saw such an object but gives an imperfect description. Gill agrees this was not the literal opening seen at Christ’s baptism or Stephen’s stoning but a visionary one, an emblem of the calling of the Gentiles. Calvin makes the same distinction, that Stephen saw heaven opened to behold the glory of Christ, whereas Peter saw the visible heaven divided so that a sheet might come from it. Clarke goes the other way and treats it as genuine perception: Peter’s mind, entirely spiritualized, was capable of discoveries of a spiritual world which surrounds us always with its plenitude of inhabitants, though we cannot see it through the dense medium of flesh and blood. Ellicott supplies a motive for its content, that one looking from Joppa across the Great Sea toward the Isles of the Gentiles might well ask how their inhabitants were to be brought into the fold. Robertson notes the historical present, and the word for sheet as an old term for linen cloth found only here.
13:
The command is disputed at the level of the verb. Clarke argues the Greek properly means sacrifice rather than slay: animals offered were given to God, and when he had received the life the flesh went back to the offerers, so that every sacrifice carried the nature of a covenant, made by eating together. Calvin refuses that reading: some pick an allegory out of the word kill, as though men were sacrificed to God by the gospel’s spiritual sword, but plainness pleases him better — God takes away the law concerning the choice of beasts, so as to teach that he rejects no people. He adds that the voice came from heaven as the sheet did, so Peter might know both were from God, the sight profiting nothing unless the voice had made clean what was unclean. Gill says the voice was formed by an angel, or rather by Christ himself. Ellicott reads it psychologically: the promptings of appetite were confirmed by the divine voice, and what resisted both was a conscience not yet freed from bondage to a ceremonial and transitory law.

The refusal is measured carefully. Robertson insists the Greek is neither a blunt refusal nor a mild protest, as Page and Furneaux argue, but a polite refusal with a reason attached. Calvin makes the same point: Peter objects to God the law God himself made, afraid to touch what it forbade; seeing a show of repugnancy between law and vision, he wants the doubt dissolved first. Barnes states the plea: the distinction stood in the Old Testament, the law remained unrepealed, and Peter, never having broken it, did not dare act otherwise. Ellicott finds the resistance to a heavenly voice strikingly in harmony with Peter’s character in the Gospels — “Be it far from thee, Lord”, “Thou shalt never wash my feet” — and notes he had been taught that what goes into the mouth cannot defile, without taking the truth in its fulness. Wesley turns the hesitation into a rule with a benefit: when God commands a strange thing the first objection often finds pardon, though it ought not to be repeated; and the delay made God’s will the more incontestable, and fitted Peter to bear his brethren’s later doubting. Clarke defines the two words — common as what was in general use among the Gentiles, unclean as what the Mosaic law forbade — and records that the rabbins and many primitive fathers held the law’s unclean animals to mean the Gentiles.

On the answer the emphasis falls on authority. Robertson notes the emphatic pronoun — do thou stop making common what God cleansed — since Peter had just called common what God invited him to eat. Clarke argues the lawgiver’s right: he who made the distinction for wise purposes may remove it when and how he pleases, and he who had authority for the first has authority for the last. Calvin extends the sentence beyond meats to all of life, since it is not for us to allow or condemn anything but for God alone, and warns that a man who makes a new difference takes to himself God’s authority. Barnes suspects Peter took the vision to mean only the abolition of the food laws, whereas the outcome showed a higher design, that those the Jews esteemed unclean were not to be so called. Ellicott presses that clean and unclean came down in the same sheet, and reads the interpretation christologically: humanity was taken up into heaven when the Eternal Word assumed man’s nature and when that nature was raised in the Ascension. Wesley makes the shortest version: nothing but what is clean can come down from heaven. Gill accounts for the threefold repetition without allegory — the voice thrice, or the sheet thrice, or both — not for any mystical meaning in the number but for Peter’s firmer assurance.
17:
The timing is what strikes the modern commentators. Barnes calls it an admirable arrangement of the events of Providence to fit each other, so ordered that the moment Peter’s mind was filled with perplexity the event occurred which relieved it. Clarke sets out the symmetry: Cornelius prays and has a vision preparing him to receive instruction from Peter, Peter prays and has one preparing him to give it, and while he is still in doubt the messengers arrive at the door. Wesley draws the rule, that things befalling us within and from without at the same time are frequently a key to each other, and such concurrences ought to be diligently attended to. Henry places the meeting in the larger design: though Paul was appointed apostle of the Gentiles and Peter of the circumcision, Peter shall break the ice and reap the first-fruits, so that believing Jews, retaining too much of the old leaven of ill-will, might be the better reconciled to their admission.

Peter’s perplexity is described with some precision. Robertson takes the verb as an intensive compound meaning to be completely at a loss which road to take, and observes that once out of the ecstasy Peter was more puzzled than ever; the word for his thinking occurs nowhere else and pictures him revolving the vision through and through. Gill records that Beza’s most ancient copy reads as though the doubting began when he came to himself, having been before as it were out of himself in the trance. Ellicott states the question exactly: a doubt might well arise whether the vision’s teaching went beyond its immediate scope, since Peter might grant it abrogated the distinction of meats and still hesitate whether it did more. Calvin makes the delay a mirror of our slackness — Peter was taught by the vision and by the word of God, yet in seeing he saw not until the Spirit became his interpreter; and we are far unlike him, many interpretations scarcely sufficing us.

The voice that resolves it is heard differently from the first. Ellicott holds the words imply a state between the trance now past and ordinary waking life, the voice no longer coming from heaven to the outward ear but heard as not less divine in the soul’s secret recesses. Wesley marks the gradualness — step by step Peter was prepared for this new admonition — and generalises it, that God leads his children on by degrees, always giving light for the present hour. Ellicott adds that the command answered the disciple’s own questionings: for a time he was to walk as if blindfold, trusting the hand that guided him, not knowing yet what his Lord was doing but to know hereafter. Robertson notes the aorist imperative bids him get down at once and the present bids him go on, and that the phrase for doubting nothing is a compound for a divided mind. Calvin says scripture uses that word often to express what sort the obedience of faith should be, as Paul commends Abraham for not doubting the promise of seed though aged and past hope, and condemns doubting consciences about meats.

Robertson notes the messengers called in a loud voice so those inside might hear, and that the verb for their enquiry is imperfect, so they kept on asking; Gill adds that they asked the people of the house in a civil and courteous manner. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the whole episode as an instance of the Spirit’s power in the apostle, placing it beside the healing of Aeneas the paralytic at Lydda and the raising of Tabitha at Joppa: being on the housetop in a trance he saw heaven opened, and by the vessel let down like a sheet full of beasts of every shape and sort he learnt plainly what he had not understood before.
23:
Chrysostom notices the hospitality before the journey: it is good that Peter first treats the men kindly after their travel and makes them at home, and only on the morrow sets out. He sees Providence in the companions, who were to be witnesses when Peter had to justify himself; Robertson agrees the wisdom of taking these six becomes manifest later at Jerusalem, and Clarke that on no slight evidence would even converted Jews accept what was coming. Ellicott gives the rule behind the number, that in the mouth of two or three witnesses every word might be established. Barnes counts four days from the angel to Caesarea, and Gill reckons the last stage at one day and part of another. Calvin makes the promptness the lesson: Peter, overcome by God’s authority, deliberates no longer, and so must we, since after we know his will nothing remains but to run where he calls.

The household gathered to meet him draws comment. Clarke notes the Syriac distinguishes kinsmen, domestics and friends, so Cornelius had gathered his whole circle; Ellicott supposes them, like his soldiers and slaves, already in sympathy with him; Barnes makes it a rule, that a man may do vast good by calling his kindred to hear the gospel; Wesley notes Cornelius did no secular business during that solemn time.

The prostration is the passage’s difficulty. Barnes and Clarke keep it civil: in Oriental countries it was usual to prostrate oneself before men of rank, and Clarke suggests that, Peter’s coming having been announced by an angel, Cornelius may have taken him for an angel of superior order. Ellicott calls it the extremest form of Eastern homage, compares Jairus before Jesus and John before the angel, and reads Peter’s refusal as treating it as homage God alone could claim — in strong contrast, he adds, with the ceremonial of those who claim to be his successors. Wesley makes the same charge in a sentence, that Peter was a man and not God, who alone ought to be worshipped, and asks whether his pretended successors have attended to this. Calvin asks formally whether Peter refuses the honour only for modesty or disallows it as unlawful, and infers from the reason he gives that something divine was offered in it. Barnes denies that Peter supposed religious reverence was meant, and takes the refusal, with Doddridge, as offering all the respect due in civil life.

On the rule Peter cites, the witnesses agree it was custom rather than statute. Robertson states it flatly: no Old Testament regulation forbids such social contact, though the rabbis added it and made it binding by custom, and nothing is more binding on the average person than social custom. Barnes agrees it was not explicitly enjoined by Moses but seemed implied, the design being to keep Israel separate by forbidding alliances with idolatrous nations — a command afterwards perverted into a ban on intercourse of every kind. Ellicott says Peter speaks from traditional Pharisaism rather than the Law, and describes the practice: the strict Jew would not enter a Gentile’s house, share a couch, or eat from the same vessel. Calvin faces the awkwardness of the opening, which might exasperate rather than win the hearers, and explains it as necessary lest they suspect Peter of an evil conscience for coming against the fathers’ custom. Clarke marks the turn: Peter now begins to understand the vision, a Gentile not being avoided for being a Gentile, and God taking down the partition wall. Wesley notes he speaks sparingly of his own former doubt. On the closing question Gill and Barnes take the readiness as the point, without objecting or making excuse; Robertson glosses it as without answering back, Peter having stepped over the line of Jewish custom; Clarke and Wesley agree that Peter, though already told the reason, invites the story afresh so the whole company may hear it.
30:
The chronology is worked out several ways from one phrase. Robertson reckons backwards from the fourth day, and notes the clause about the hour has an accusative of extent, so Cornelius kept the whole ninth hour of prayer. Wesley lays the days out in order: the vision, the messengers reaching Joppa, Peter setting out, the arrival at Caesarea. Barnes fixes the hour at three in the afternoon, and notes that the figure called an angel earlier is here called a man, since that was his appearance. Clarke calculates the fast as running from three o’clock the preceding day to three on this one, and denies that Cornelius fasted four days together — and even if he did, he ate one meal on each. Ellicott declines to fix the hour but argues from the practice of devout Jews that the vision may have fallen on the second day of the week and Peter’s on the fifth, so the meeting probably took place on the Sabbath.

The word for fasting is itself in dispute, and the two who raise it take opposite sides. Clarke reports it wanting in several of the best manuscripts and in the Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Vulgate. Calvin, writing long before, notes the old interpreter omitted the word and judges this done through error or negligence, since it stands in all the Greek books he knows; and he explains that Cornelius mentions the fast partly so we may know he did not pray coldly or perfunctorily. Calvin adds that the speech is otherwise a bare repetition of the history, whose sum is that Cornelius called Peter at God’s commandment.

On the answer to the prayer the witnesses differ over what was asked. Wesley supposes he had been praying for instruction how to worship God most acceptably. Ellicott notes the singular here is more definite than the plural earlier and infers a prayer for fuller light — a man who had heard, through Philip at Caesarea or the brother-officer once at Capernaum, of the teaching and life of Jesus, might well seek guidance about the terms of admission. Gill takes it of the prayer then being made as well as those offered before. Clarke turns it into a rule about using light already given: Cornelius prayed, fasted and gave alms, and looked for salvation this way — not to purchase it, a thought which never entered his mind, but as the means of bringing his soul to the truth; he used the light God had given, and God increased his gifts mightily.

The closing courtesies are read as more than courtesy. Ellicott observes that thou hast well done was in social usage an expression of heartfelt gratitude rather than mere approval; Robertson calls it a regular formula for thanks, adding that Cornelius commends Peter’s courage in breaking from Jewish custom and takes no offence at the implied superiority of Jew over Gentile. Gill finds in the promptness a disclaimer of pride, since Cornelius did not send of his own motion but by a divine order executed the same hour. Barnes reads the last clause as implying they believed God saw them, were assembled at his command, and were disposed to listen. Ellicott hears both readiness and anxiety, the circle sharing Cornelius’s solicitude and willing to obey whatever came as God’s command while hoping it would not lay on them too heavy a burden. Calvin explains why it is said at all, that a teacher is much moved to take pains when sure his hearers will profit, and leaves open whether the words are an oath or a simple profession that the company was gathered as in God’s sight. Clarke records that several versions read before thee rather than before God, and pictures the people waiting for the preacher with every heart filled with expectation. Wesley gives it the widest application, calling it the language of every truly Christian congregation.
34:
The opening formula is itself noticed. Henry treats what follows as an abstract, since Peter must have testified with many other words, and finds in the phrase a mark of solemnity combined with freedom and copiousness. Calvin says scripture uses it wherever a weighty oration is meant, as when Jesus opened his mouth to preach to his disciples. Robertson calls it a solemn formula and also good elocution, and notes the verb for perceiving is a middle denoting mental action — something Peter had found hard to grasp until now.

On the principle announced they agree, then divide over how far it reaches. Barnes defines the term as showing favour for rank, family or wealth, as a partial judge does, and takes the next verse as the ground: God’s favours are not confined to the Jew but extend to all on the same principle. Clarke denies partiality both ways, God neither esteeming a Jew for being a Jew nor detesting a Gentile for being one, the contrary having been a deeply rooted opinion among the Jews — Peter’s own until the vision. Ellicott notes Peter had already seen that absence of respect of persons in his Master, and that James presses the same quality, but that both had still to learn its wider application. Robertson states the conclusion narrowly: a Gentile need not become a Jew to become a Christian, which Peter had not perceived before, since at Pentecost, speaking of the promise to those afar off, he had understood they must first become Jews — this new idea making a revolution in his outlook. Wesley reaches further: in a particular sense God does not confine his love to one nation, in a general he is loving to every man and wills all to be saved. Gill extends the reach to any Gentile nation, even to Scythia.

The clause about being accepted produces the sharpest division in the chapter. Clarke reads it as a description of character: in every nation the man who, according to his light, fears God and worships him alone, works righteousness and injures neither the body, soul nor reputation of his neighbour is accepted — not the nation, kindred, profession or form of worship being what the just God regards, but the character. Wesley presses it hardest, defining the two terms — reverencing God as the cause, end and governor of all, and from that regard not only avoiding known evil but endeavouring by the best light he has to do all things well — and concluding that such a man is accepted through Christ though he does not know him, the assertion admitting no exception. Ellicott agrees it applies not only to those who know the name of Christ but to all who in any age or country fear God according to their knowledge and work righteousness according to their opportunities. Calvin takes the two terms as comprehending the integrity of the whole life, the fear of God being godliness and the other the equity men use among themselves. Barnes and Robertson keep the statement to the point at issue, that God’s favours are not restricted by nation.

The sermon proper begins, and its first sentence resists construction. Gill marks the transition, what preceded being only a preface, and takes the word sent to Israel as the gospel, sent first to the Jews by the apostles. Barnes reports few passages in the New Testament have perplexed critics more, since it is hard to say what the accusative refers to, and warns that the English misleads by making it identical with the next verse. Cyril of Jerusalem quotes the verse to establish that the Son of God is Lord, he who was born at Bethlehem according to the angel’s word to the shepherds; and on the baptism that follows he sets herald against King: John was great, but what is he to the Lord?
39:
The claim to be a witness is made twice in different senses, and Calvin marks the shift: Peter first says he and his fellows saw with their own eyes all they report, and shortly after uses the word of an office, they being appointed witnesses by God. Robertson notes the appeal runs both ways, to what the audience know and to what the disciples know, and that Peter made the same claim at Pentecost. Clarke suggests it may take in not only the twelve but the six brethren Peter had brought. Ellicott hears the commission given at the opening of the book, and argues that ‘the land of the Jews’, spoken at Caesarea by a Galilean, bears the narrower sense of Judea — implying a ministry the first three Gospels barely record. Gill takes the witnessing to cover Christ’s going about, the good he did and the miracles he wrought.

On the death the concern is evidential. Barnes corrects the translation, which seems to describe two acts of slaying and suspending, whereas the original says they put him to death by suspending him on a tree, the cross. Clarke gives the reason the death is stated: the truth of the resurrection depending on the reality of the death, this had to rest on indubitable evidence. On the interval he argues both ways — Christ lay long enough to prove he was dead, and not so long that the disciples could be supposed to have had time for deceit, the tomb being guarded throughout. Gill notes the resurrection, though sometimes ascribed to Christ himself as God, is here as generally ascribed to the Father. Barnes reads the showing openly as leaving no room for deception, Ellicott renders it literally as giving him to be manifest, and Robertson calls the phrase peculiar and found only here and in Romans.

Why the appearances were restricted is the difficulty, and each answers differently. Barnes says a general appearance was not necessary to establish the resurrection, Christ having shown himself to many. Gill takes the exclusion to fall on those who crucified him, and notes that not even all Christians saw him, though five hundred did at once. Clarke explains it from the purpose of the interval: the public were no longer to be instructed by Christ in person, so the time after the resurrection went to furnishing the preachers, God choosing the witnesses best qualified to attest the fact. Calvin declines to answer from necessity: though no reason could be shown, God’s counsel alone ought to suffice sober men — yet he used this moderation to a good end, the resurrection being proved by many firm testimonies while the restraint exercised faith. Robertson makes the restriction itself evidence, calling it the historian’s candour: Peter states the thing as it happened instead of claiming that friends and foes alike saw the risen Christ. On the eating and drinking, Barnes says it furnished the clearest proof, Ellicott names the three recorded instances and calls it the crucial test that what the disciples saw was no phantom, and Wesley glosses it as conversing familiarly with him.

The sermon closes on judgment and forgiveness. Wesley takes the appointment as Judge of quick and dead to cover all men, whether alive at his coming or dead before, declaring in the strongest terms how entirely the hearers’ happiness depended on a timely and humble subjection. On the last verse he notes that Peter, speaking to heathens, quotes no prophet in particular, and that the promise runs to everyone who believes, Jew or Gentile — adding a qualification that cuts against his own earlier reading, that such a man receives remission though he had not before feared God or worked righteousness. Robertson describes the word for the chosen witnesses as a double compound meaning designated beforehand, as old as Plato but occurring only here; Ellicott prefers to render it appointed.
44:
The interruption is read as deliberate. Chrysostom sets out the management: God does not suffer the speech to be finished, nor the baptism to follow a command of Peter, but waits until it is evident how admirable their state of mind is and teaching has begun — then the Spirit comes at once, so disposed as to give Peter a mighty ground to stand on afterwards. Henry says much the same, that Peter did not labour in vain but was happily superseded while still speaking and perhaps intending to say more, God owning his word by conferring the Spirit on the hearers at once. Robertson notes the construction shows the speaking still going on and Peter plainly interrupted; Clarke thinks it unlikely the recorded words are all he spoke. Calvin calls it a new miracle declaring the gospel common to Gentiles and Jews, and an excellent seal of the Gentile calling, since the Lord would never have bestowed the graces of his Spirit except to declare they too were adopted into the covenant — adding that these gifts differ from the grace of regeneration. Wesley calls them consecrated as the first fruits of the Gentiles, and takes the event as evidence that God had accepted them as well as the Jews; Barnes notes Peter makes much of this in the next chapter.

What the tongues were is disputed, and the division is clean. Gill takes them for tongues the speakers had never learned, in which they spoke of the wonderful works of God as the apostles had at Pentecost; Barnes says languages other than their native one; Clarke says the descent was known by their speaking with different kinds of tongues, though how the gift was bestowed we cannot tell. Ellicott reads the same words differently: they imply a sudden thrill of spiritual joy showing itself in a burst of unpremeditated praise, the tongues appearing not as instruments of teaching but in magnifying God — and he observes that nothing here says the utterance was in any language other than those the speakers already knew. Clarke adds a remark that belongs to either reading, that they had got new hearts as well as new tongues.

The astonishment of Peter’s companions is taken as evidence. Ellicott says Luke dwells on it as a testimony beyond suspicion to the gift’s reality, since those who came with Peter were not sharers in the joy they were compelled to recognise as the Spirit’s work, listening with amazement as the rapturous chant burst from heathens not yet baptised — one definite fulfilment, he says, of Peter’s vision. Clarke explains the amazement from a settled maxim, that the divine influence could not be revealed beyond the precincts of the promised land, and that none of them believed the Spirit could be given to a Gentile at all. Barnes puts it more simply, that they were amazed Gentiles should be admitted to the same favour; Robertson glosses the word as standing out of oneself, the weight falling on the Spirit being poured out even upon Gentiles. Calvin finds the amazement itself strange, since they knew Peter had been sent by God, and turns the difficulty into a remark about charity: Luke calls men faithful who were still held by a wicked error, for the Lord does not at once wipe away every cloud of ignorance, and such clouds do not darken the praise of faith before God, who pardons the errors.

The baptism follows as a conclusion nobody resists. Cyril of Jerusalem supplies the reason water is still required after the Spirit has come: since man is of twofold nature, soul and body, the purification is twofold also, the water cleansing the body and the Spirit sealing the soul, so that we draw near to God with the heart sprinkled by the Spirit and the body washed with pure water.
